title: Satellite operators are in panic mode due to a worsening launch crisis
gist: Despite record launch cadence, satellite operators face a worsening launch-capacity crunch driven by SpaceX's plan to wind down commercial Falcon 9 flights (possibly after 2028), stalled competitors (Vulcan, New Glenn), and surging constellation demand—with experts warning the shortage becomes acute around 2028.

themes.theme: Launch capacity crunch and surging demand

insights.claim: Satellite operators including Telesat, Amazon LEO, and AST SpaceMobile are competing for scarce launch slots, with AST calling launch availability the pacing item for deploying its constellation.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Launch scarcity is now the binding constraint on constellation deployment—a bottleneck that advantages incumbents with booked slots and rewards new launch entrants.
insights.quote: What we have is an industry in panic
insights.locator: As part of his job as the director of research at Quilty Space

insights.claim: Analysys Mason forecasts more than 37,000 satellites will need to be launched between 2023 and 2033, and the Commercial Space Federation predicts demand for thousands of launches annually within a decade.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Quantifies a demand wall that vastly exceeds current supply, framing launch as a structural growth market.
insights.quote: more than 37,000 satellites will need to be launched between 2023 and 2033

themes.theme: SpaceX priorities shifting away from commercial launch

insights.claim: SpaceX intends to wind down Falcon 9 as fast as possible in favor of Starship and has told the US government it plans to end commercial launches after 2028, prioritizing its own Starlink v3 satellites and orbital data centers over third-party payloads.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The dominant Western launch provider is deprioritizing the commercial market, leaving operators unable to plan around Falcon 9—a major opening for competitors.
insights.quote: SpaceX has told the US government that it intends to end commercial launches after 2028

insights.claim: In Q2 2026 a majority of SpaceX revenue ($4.3B of $7.8B) came from Starlink, while less than 12 percent came from space services of which commercial launch is only a fraction.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Reveals commercial launch is economically trivial to SpaceX, explaining why it will deprioritize it in favor of vertically integrated Starlink revenue.
insights.quote: A majority of the company's revenue ($4.3 billion out of $7.8 billion) during the second quarter of 2026 came from Starlink

themes.theme: Geopolitics: Ukraine war removed Russian launch

insights.claim: Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine removed Soyuz and Proton rockets from the Western market just as Ariane 5-to-6 and Atlas V-to-Vulcan transitions left incumbents short, leaving SpaceX's Falcon 9 to backstop the entire Western Hemisphere's launch needs.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Geopolitical shock created SpaceX's near-monopoly on Western launch; concentration risk remains until competitors scale.
insights.quote: Without SpaceX, the Western launch market would have been completely screwed over the last half-decade.

insights.claim: Vulcan has flown only two military missions six years after its Space Force award due to Northrop Grumman solid-booster problems, and Blue Origin's New Glenn is offline until at least late 2026 after a May static-fire explosion destroyed its only launch pad.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The two heavy-lift SpaceX alternatives are both badly behind, extending Falcon 9 dependence and delaying competitive relief.
insights.locator: Waiting on Vulcan and New Glenn

insights.claim: A new generation of US medium-lift reusables—Stoke Space's Nova, Rocket Lab's Neutron, Relativity's Terran R, and Firefly/Northrop's Eclipse—target debuts around 2027 but will take years to reach meaningful cadence.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Names the pipeline of challengers investors can track; none will relieve the crunch quickly.

insights.claim: Stoke Space's Devon Papandrew predicts the launch crisis becomes really acute around 2028 even if all four medium-lift entrants hit their goals.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Sets a timeline: the supply gap peaks near 2028, a window of pricing power for whoever can fly.
insights.quote: I think 2028 is when this problem becomes really acute
insights.locator: Stoke's vice president of business development

insights.claim: Policy experts float but discount ideas of forcing SpaceX to sell Falcon 9 infrastructure or nationalizing it, noting the hardware works because of SpaceX engineers and that Elon Musk's political capital makes coercion unlikely.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Nationalization tail-risk is low; any government action would need to be mutually agreeable, so Falcon 9's fate stays in SpaceX's hands.
insights.quote: Any government effort in this area to keep Falcon 9 flying would have to be mutually agreeable and beneficial to both parties
